overview.description: MakaÃ³ (often referred to as 'Mak-Var' in regional contexts) is the most popular shedding card game in Hungary and much of Central Europe. It is the tactical ancestor of games like Uno and Crazy Eights. Using a standard 32-card or 52-card deck, players attempt to discard all their cards while using powerful action cards to penalize opponents. The game's name comes from the requirement to shout 'MakaÃ³!' when one card remains.

history.origins: Derived from the European 'Mau-Mau' family of games. It gained its distinct 'MakaÃ³' rules in the early 20th century as a more aggressive variant.
timeline: 1920s: Mau-Mau variants become popular in Budapest cafes.
1960s: Standardized rules for 'King-Double' and 'Seven-Chain' are adopted.
Present: The quintessential childhood and family game in Hungary, often exported to neighboring regions under similar names like 'Makao' (Poland).
history.evolution: While modern 'Uno' simplified the deck, MakaÃ³ maintains the use of standard cards where ranks (2, 3, 4, 7, Ace, King) have specific, non-intuitive rules.
history.cultural: Commonly played in schools, on trains, and at pub tables across Hungary.

setup.deck: Standard 52 cards (for many players) or 32 cards (for few).

rules.objective: Be the first player to discard all cards from your hand.
rules.gameplay:
1. Play a card that matches either the **suit** or the **rank** of the top card on the pile.
2. If you cannot play, draw one card from the deck.
keyRules: Play a card matching the top card's suit or rank; Ace and Joker are wild.
If you cannot play, draw one card from the deck.
When down to one card you must call 'Makaó'; if an opponent calls first you draw 5.

Action cards: 2 (next draws 2, stackable), 3 (next draws 3, stackable), 4 (next misses a turn, stackable), Jack (call a value), King Spades/Hearts (draw 5 or stack), Joker (reverse direction), Ace (call new suit).

strategy.basic: Save your Aces. An Ace is your 'get out of jail free' card when you don't have the current suit. Don't play it too early unless you can switch the suit to one where you have a long sequence.
strategy.intermediate: Stacking Mastery: If you have two 2s and a 3, wait until someone plays a 2 on YOU. Stack your 2s back at them to force them (or the next person) to draw 7 cards. This is the primary way to win a 'losing' game.
strategy.advanced: The 'Seven-Stop' Defense: If you suspect the player before you is about to play a 'Draw 5' King, hold your 7 of any suit. It is the only way to nullify a high-draw penalty and seize the lead.
tips: Count the 2s and 3s. If all four 2s are played, the 'Draw' danger is significantly reduced.
If you holding a 5, check if your house rules allow 'Multi-5' discarding (playing multiple 5s in one turn).

edgeCases.text: Player with one card must call 'Makaó' before next player acts; if an opponent calls first, the player draws 5.
2s and 3s stack: multiple 2s or 3s played in sequence add (next player draws 2 or 3 per card); 4s stack to skip multiple turns.
King of Spades targets the previous player (draw 5); King of Hearts targets the next player; Queen of Hearts can deflect.
7 can nullify a King draw-5 penalty in some house rules.
Runs: consecutive same-suit cards may be played in one turn; may switch suit at same rank.
